newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela struts reforms, skeptics yawn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela struts reforms, skeptics yawn.

text.p: Venezuela is moving into public relations over-drive to convince skeptics that the wide-ranging economic reforms of the past year were no flash in the pan.

Culminating a day of cautious self-congratulation, three government ministers appeared on a prime-time radio and television broadcast Tuesday night to laud the success of the economic reform program called the Venezuelan Agenda.

The Venezuelan Agenda "is an advertising slogan with no real content," said Carmelo Lauria, president of the Chamber of Deputies' Finance Committee and a leader of the opposition Accion Democratica (AD) party.
He said little would have been achieved without a fortunate oil bonanza from higher international crude prices.
"It was just a propaganda operation ... laced with a few lies, including one that inflation is defeated", said Agustin Berrios, a secretary general of Christian Democrat Copei party.

Overlaid with graphics of a rippling Venezuelan flag, the Planning, Finance and Trade and Industry ministers delivered separate straight-faced speeches, interspersed with footage of President Rafael Caldera shaking hands, kissing children, signing agreements, opening dams and gazing towards the horizon.
"We're moving towards a more productive, efficient, more competitive Venezuela," a businesslike Trade and Industry Minister Freddy Rojas Parra said.

"Inflation has been completely beaten," Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar said in a 10-minute spot which reviewed the effects of reforms launched on April 15, 1996 that saw exchange rates freed, prices liberalized and taxes raised.

"Armed with the will to work and the knowledge that nothing can be achieved without sacrifice, we're going to get out of the mists that have clouded this country for so long," Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff exhorted listeners and viewers.
The broadcast capped a day of media frenzy that saw ministers stress to a recession-ravaged public the social component of the reforms, while also candidly admitting that much remained to be done.

"What has been achieved hitherto is only a start," echoed International Monetary Fund managing director Michel Camdessus in a special supplement Wednesday in leading daily El Nacional. "It's necessary not only to continue, but also to deepen the reforms begun with Venezuelan Agenda. Otherwise, what has been gained will only prove ephemeral," he wrote.

A number of ambitious structural reforms -- notably privatization of parastatal Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana's (CVG) huge iron and steel companies -- are planned for the remaining two years of Caldera's administration.

But unlike the macroeconomic successes of the past year, which were executed with the stroke of a pen, analysts say they involve difficult maneuvering by a minority government through fragile coalitions.
